Q-learning

One change to SARSA: in the target, use the best next action instead of the one the agent will actually take. The target then estimates the optimal action values $q_*$ directly, whatever the agent does while exploring. Learning about one policy while following another is called off-policy learning.

Learn from a random walker

S&B's 4×4 gridworld (Example 4.1): grey corners are terminal, every step costs $-1$. A walker picks uniformly random moves, starting each episode in a random cell. SARSA and Q-learning learn from the same stream of experience, with $\alpha = 0.1$.

Errors are root-mean-square over the 14 cells. $v_\pi$ is the random policy's value (S&B Figure 4.1, $-14$ to $-22$). $v_*$ is minus the distance to the nearest corner. Same data, different targets, different answers. SARSA needs a few thousand episodes to get close; Q-learning needs a few hundred.

The maths

The Q-learning update (Watkins, 1989):

$$Q(S_t, A_t) \leftarrow Q(S_t, A_t) + \alpha\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_a Q(S_{t+1}, a) - Q(S_t, A_t)\big]$$

Compare SARSA, which uses $Q(S_{t+1}, A_{t+1})$. Here the target takes the best next action according to the current $Q$, whether or not the agent takes it.

The target is a sample of the Bellman optimality equation for action values (Lesson 29):

$$q_*(s, a) = \mathbb{E}\big[R_{t+1} + \gamma \max_{a'} q_*(S_{t+1}, a') \,\big|\, S_t = s, A_t = a\big]$$

The expectation is only over the environment's response $p(s', r \mid s, a)$. No policy appears in it. So it does not matter which policy chose $A_t$: any transition from $(s, a)$ is a valid sample. The policy that generates data (the behaviour policy) can explore freely while $Q$ learns about the greedy policy (the target policy).

Q-learning converges to $q_*$ with probability 1 provided every pair $(s, a)$ keeps being updated and the step sizes satisfy

$$\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \alpha_n = \infty, \qquad \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \alpha_n^2 < \infty$$

The first condition lets the steps overcome any starting values. The second makes them small enough that the noise averages out (Lesson 7). A constant $\alpha$ breaks the second, so estimates keep fluctuating, but they stay close.

In the random-walker demo, SARSA's $A_{t+1}$ comes from the random policy, so it learns $q_\pi$ of that policy, and $\sum_a \pi(a \mid s) Q(s, a)$ approaches $v_\pi$ (Lesson 23). Q-learning's $\max$ ignores how badly the walker behaves and approaches $v_*(s) = \max_a q_*(s, a)$.
